query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small, controlled amount of an oxidizable element (Ti) into an AlCoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloy—implemented via a laser cladding process to produce an AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 surface coating—will trigger the in situ formation of a stable, self-adaptive oxide film that acts as a lubricating barrier, thereby reducing both the coefficient of friction and wear rate over a wide temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: An untreated AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with a conventional multiphase or near single‐phase microstructure lacking a continuous, protective oxide film.
generation.intervention: Laser cladding deposition of an AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 coating (i.e. incorporating approximately 0.5 atom% Ti) that is designed to promote controlled oxide formation during service.
generation.conditions: Dry sliding wear conditions across a broad service temperature range (from room temperature up to approximately 900°C) under atmospherical conditions where oxidation is possible.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined multiphase microstructure with well‐distributed Ti-rich regions that, upon sliding, rapidly form a continuous, protective oxide film serving as a solid lubricant.
generation.mechanism: The incorporated Ti has a high oxygen affinity so that during sliding—even at low temperatures—a thin, adherent oxide layer forms on the coating’s surface. This layer acts as a barrier to direct metal‐to‐metal contact, reducing friction and wear. At higher temperatures, the oxide grows to a stable state that maintains lubrication despite increased mechanical and thermal stresses.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated HEA, the Ti-doped, laser cladded coating will show a lower friction coefficient (estimated reduction on the order of 15–25%, though the exact value is uncertain) and a substantially reduced wear rate across the entire temperature range, as the self-forming oxide continuously protects the surface.
generation.baseline: Friction and wear performance measured in prior studies on untreated conformal AlCoCrFeNi HEAs (e.g., in room- to high-temperature wear tests where protective oxide films form only gradually or incompletely).
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect relies on the environment being sufficiently oxidative; in strongly reducing atmospheres or under extreme mechanical loads beyond the coating’s integrity, the oxide layer might not form or adhere properly, limiting the effect.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative improvements (in percentage terms, for example) are not precisely known and could vary with the exact Ti content, processing parameters, and testing conditions. Furthermore, while protective oxide formation has been observed at high temperatures, its robustness at lower temperatures requires further verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: one set consisting of the Ti-doped (AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5) coating produced via laser cladding and a control set of the standard AlCoCrFeNi HEA. Conduct systematic pin-on-disc tribological tests over a temperature range from room temperature to 900°C under identical dry sliding conditions. Employ surface characterization (e.g., SEM, XRD) to check for the presence and integrity of the oxide film.
measurements: Coefficient of friction at various temperatures
Wear rate (volume loss per unit load and sliding distance)
Microstructural and surface chemical analysis of the worn surfaces to verify oxide film formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-doped coating does not show a statistically significant reduction in both coefficient of friction and wear rate across the tested temperature range compared with the control alloy—or if a continuous, protective oxide layer is not detected on the worn surface—the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-Temperature Wear Behaviour of Spark Plasma Sintered AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 High-Entropy Alloy

Abstract: AbstractIn this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrF
